text: Hardening one server by hand — working through a benchmark, writing a sysctl file, locking down SSH — is a reasonable afternoon's work. Hardening fifty servers the same way is fifty afternoons, and at that scale two things start happening that manual, one-host-at-a-time work simply can't catch: new hosts come up unhardened from a base image, and existing hosts quietly drift from their original compliant state.

That drift is real even when nobody deliberately changes a setting. A patch resets a config file to its package default. An engineer edits sshd_config directly during an outage at 2 a.m. and never reapplies the hardening on top. A reinstall silently re-enables a kernel module that was disabled. Six months later, a fleet that started 95% compliant could be anywhere, and nobody can say which hosts are which without re-scanning every one.

The first real fix is a shell script, checked into version control, that applies the last two lessons' settings — not as a one-time run, but idempotent: it checks current state before changing anything, so running it twice produces the same result as running it once, instead of blindly re-appending the same line every time.

The second fix removes the last manual step entirely. Ansible runs a single playbook against an inventory of however many hosts, applying the same role to all of them over SSH. The real ansible-lockdown project ships CIS Benchmark controls exactly this way — each numbered recommendation as its own tagged task — and --check mode reports what would change before anything actually does.

A nightly check-mode run flags three app servers where SYN cookies silently reverted after a routine patch rebuilt their sysctl config from the package default. Running the same playbook for real that night puts them back in compliance before anyone finds out the hard way during an actual attack. Next up: a fleet this disciplined can still run a single container with none of it applied.
